Here are our trail recipes for long-distance hikes!
The quantities in the recipes are for an average portion; you can add/reduce to taste and according to how hungry you are.
Nutritious and tasty oatmeal porridge
Ingredients for one portion:
– 4 tablespoons fine rolled oats
– 0.75 cup water
– 1 tablespoon milk powder
– 1 teaspoon sugar
– some dried fruit/nuts for an upgrade
Preparation:
1. Boil 0.75 cup of water.
2. Meanwhile, mix all the dry ingredients in a bowl.
3. Once the water has boiled, add the hot water to the bowl – and stir well.
Buddha bowl
Ingredients for one portion:
– a third/half cup of rice (depending on hunger)
– nori seaweed for sushi
– soy sauce
– salt to taste
– you can add a piece of vegetable such as cabbage, pepper, carrot, etc.
Preparation:
1. Boil water in a quantity twice that of the rice.
2. Once the water is boiling, add the rice and seasonings, stir and cover.
3. Continue cooking over low heat for 15 minutes.
4. At the end of the cooking time, turn off the heat and let the pot rest for a few minutes.
5. Chop the vegetable (if you have one) and mix it with the rice in the bowl/pot.
6. Tear the sushi seaweed by hand, mix with the rice and add soy sauce.
Indulgent risotto
Ingredients for one portion:
– a handful of dried mushrooms
– half/a third cup of rice (depending on hunger)
– a piece of high-fat cheese, such as processed cheese of any kind or hard cheese
– salt to taste
– olive oil
– a small disposable plastic bottle
– a knife
Preparation:
1. 6 hours before the meal, put the dried mushrooms into a small plastic bottle and fill it with water to the top. Close the bottle tightly with the cap and "forget" about it until mealtime.
2. Fill the pot with the mushroom water and the mushrooms (you can cut the bottle open for this), and bring the water to a boil with the mushrooms inside.
3. Once the water has boiled, add olive oil, and then the rice.
4. Make sure the rice is covered with water at all times, and continue cooking and stirring until the rice is done.
5. When the rice is cooked and hot, add the processed cheese and stir.
Trail bulgur salad
Ingredients for one portion:
– half a cup of bulgur
– half a cucumber
– a tomato
– a little olive oil
– lemon juice (if available)
– salt and pepper to taste

– a knife

Understand your needs Am I planning a long hike on the Israel National Trail? Am I looking for a pack for day hikes? Based on that, we will try to understand what need the pack is meant to meet, and thus work out the desired volume and which features are more or less important. Below you will find explanations and information about the various properties and features, and about the right way to plan the packing of your gear inside the pack.
It is important to understand that a week-and-a-half trip will require a pack volume similar to one suited to a two-month trip. This is because in any case we will stock up on food and water as we walk, and we will wash our clothes during the trip.
Make a list of the items that should go into the pack Once we have understood our needs, we will work out what needs to be packed. The idea is to understand how much space all these items will take up. Remember that some gear takes up more volume, such as a sleeping bag, mattress, cooking kit, etc.
Based on the expected quantity and size of the gear that will go into the pack, we can choose the appropriate volume. Preparing a list in advance will prevent disappointment. If we buy a pack that is too small, we will have to hang many items on the outside of the pack, which will get in the way of walking. On the other hand, if we buy a pack that is too big – we will probably be tempted to fill it with non-essential gear that adds unnecessary weight to our back. Below we explain how it is recommended to plan the gear you need.
Straps Hiking packs are usually loaded with straps from every compartment and in every direction, and it is very easy to get lost. But there are several straps worth knowing:
– The hip belt is designed to ensure that the pack's weight is split between the shoulders and the hips, so make sure it closes without pressing on the stomach and "sits" on us well.
– The pack's shoulder straps put the weight on the shoulders, and the straps above them are meant to pull the upper part of the pack toward the shoulder blades when needed.
– Beyond these, when trying on the pack make sure all the other straps on the pack are closed and tightened, which "packs" the pack and compresses it.
Features After we have tried on the pack with weight and volume and made sure the main straps are comfortable and suit us, we move on to features. Here there is no limit to creativity: a compartment for a hydration bladder, a compartment for water bottles on the side or front, small pockets for snacks, compartments for sandals, a zipper along the sides of the pack so it opens like a suitcase, straps for tying on a mattress, and what not.

נבדוק מה מסתתר מתחת לאף אחותך חזרה מהטיו:
Check what is hiding right under your nose Has your sister come back from her big trip and no longer uses her backpack? Is there a pack your uncle does not need hiding in his storeroom? Our acquaintances may well have an unused hiking pack at home that could suit us.
Join second-hand groups Like many other hobbies, hiking may also require buying expensive gear. Buying second-hand will be cheaper – and more ecological too. The second-hand market for hiking gear in Israel offers a range of products, even if it is not as developed as abroad, and the groups on the subject are active mainly on Facebook.
Try packs on properly in the store If we have chosen to buy in a store, the chance of choosing the most suitable pack grows the more packs we try on, and the better we understand what is more or less comfortable for us. There are many brands on the market offering packs with a variety of back systems suited to different body types. For example, people with a narrow, short build will suit a different back system than people with a broad, tall build.
When trying on a pack in the store, ask to add weight to the pack. Most outdoor stores keep sandbags of various weights, and if there are none, you can fill the pack with relatively heavy, bulky products. Trying on the pack with weight inside is meant to simulate real use of the pack on the trail, which will usually include at least 3 liters of water, clothing for the season, food, a sleeping bag, cooking utensils and more. After adding weight to the pack, we may discover that a pack that seemed comfortable is not, and sometimes it turns out that the added weight makes the pack more comfortable.
The bigger the pack, the more it will weigh On long trails, the key word is minimalism – that is, carry as little as possible and try to choose the lightest gear you can. The larger the volume of the pack we choose, the greater the chance that we will fill it with non-essential things and weigh ourselves down.
More expensive is not better A hiking pack does not have to be an expensive affair, and there is a chance that an expensive pack will not suit our needs at all. Of course some brands are of higher quality than others, but in the end comfort is the deciding factor. If the pack is comfortable and sits well on us, we may have found the right pack, even if it is not made by a prestige brand.

מילת המפתח: מינימליזם ככל שנעמיס פחות הת:
The key word: minimalism The less we load, the less the pack weighs – and the more fun we will have hiking. Before packing, it is worth laying out in front of us all the items we want to take, going through them one by one and checking: is it essential? If there is an item that can be weeded out – one less shirt, one less pair of socks, etc. – don't hesitate to give it up. Remember that every unnecessary gram adds to the already heavy weight on our back and affects the quality of the trip and our enjoyment.
Plan ahead as much as possible What will we eat at each meal and what ingredients are needed? For example, instead of putting a 1 kg bag of rice in the pack, check in advance how many meals you will need, how many portions you will cook and where the next resupply point is – and accordingly pack only the necessary amount according to the plan.
The same goes for water: in the north there are many points where you can stock up on water during the day, so you can carry less water – as long as you plan ahead.
Sleeping bag The sleeping bag is without doubt one of the most important items we pack for the trip. Compress the sleeping bag as small as possible using its straps. If the sleeping bag came in a cover without straps, it is recommended to buy a compression sack, which will save us a lot of space. Most hiking packs have a bottom compartment where a compressed sleeping bag can usually be packed comfortably. In winter or on days when rain is expected, it is recommended to put the sleeping bag in a plastic bag, to make sure that when we reach the campsite in the evening we have a dry sleeping bag to get into.
Heavy items Heavy items, such as a pot, heavy food packages, etc., should be packed in the compartment above the sleeping bag compartment – as close as possible to our back and at the bottom of the compartment. This is the area where the hip belt provides good support, so it is best to place the heavy gear there. Avoid putting heavy items in the part of the pack close to the head or far from the back, to keep your balance and not overload the shoulders.
Mattress Although a camping mattress is usually lightweight compared to other items we carry on our back on the trip, it takes up a lot of volume, so it is worth thinking in advance about its place in the pack. There are two main types of camping mattress. The "egg-crate" mattress that folds like an accordion, or closed-cell foam mattresses – are usually tied on the outside, at the bottom or on the sides of the pack, using the straps. The second type is inflatable mattresses, which can be compressed like sleeping bags,

The challenges of hiking alone are many – but if the idea appeals to you, it is not worth giving up the experience. There are ways to cope with the difficulties and increase the chance that a solo hike will be not only about overcoming challenges, but also a very special kind of enjoyment.
Here are 7 tips that can help:
1. Start by thinking things over with ourselves. Try to work out the reasons that make us want to hike alone, and then answer honestly questions such as how well we know ourselves in moments of crisis and what usually helps us get through them, how comfortable we will feel in nature both in daylight and when darkness falls, whether we have hiking experience, and if so what kinds of hikes we have tried in the past, and which skills we would like to improve before setting out on such an adventure.
2. Learn basic fieldcraft skills. You don't need to be a scout instructor to hike by yourself for a week in nature, but it is worth knowing how to read a topographic map with a scale, navigate without an app, use a camping stove, pitch a tent and light a fire, for example.
3. Try a short solo hike to begin with. To get a first idea of what it feels like to hike alone, choose an easy route that includes one or two nights and requires us to carry gear on our back and sleep outdoors. Since this is a first experience, soften it with a relatively well-traveled route, where we may walk alone but will not really be alone, and will at least have the option of sleeping in the company of others.
It should be a route with cell reception and exit points along the way, in case we find the experience unpleasant, and preferably one where we can stock up on food along the way and not just water, to lift our spirits and ease the load on our back.
4. Arrange for someone at home to receive updates from us. It is important that someone at home knows in advance where and when we will be hiking, and that we update them several times a day or as much as possible. That way, in an emergency without reception, at the very least there will be someone who will make sure to look for us.
5. Learn about the area we will hike in. Unfamiliarity heightens feelings of fear and anxiety (and this is true in every area of life). Of course confidence comes with experience, but learning about the area and surroundings in advance can help. That way, if we wake up at night to unusual sounds, we will know in advance that it is most likely just a cow or a wild boar, that the howls of the jackals at dusk do not mean they are coming to devour us, and what

1. Bring your own fuel. It is important to bring fuel with us so as not to damage the local vegetation – damage that occurs even if we gather "just" a few branches from a tree or bush. In addition, it is important to avoid burning synthetic materials, or wood with a coating or chemical treatment, such as spraying against woodworm or paint.
2. Make sure lighting a fire is permitted. Before lighting a campfire, it is important to make sure that lighting fires is permitted where we are. For example, lighting fires is prohibited in nature reserves, unless signage on site explicitly states that it is permitted. Sometimes, in transitional seasons and due to unusual weather, the Fire Commissioner issues a "campfire ban order", which is published online. If we suspect that this may be such a time, it is important to check and make sure. In the era of climate change, the weather in Israel is becoming hotter and drier and there are more fire-prone days throughout the year. Extra caution is therefore required on this matter.
3. Check whether there is a designated campfire area. Some overnight campsites have designated campfire and fire-lighting areas, in order to concentrate the campfires in defined spots and keep the overnight campsite cleaner. If there is a designated fire-lighting area, it should be preferred.
4. Check whether there are remains of existing campfires. If there are no designated campfire areas, it is better to light the fire on the remains of a previous campfire. There are two reasons for this: first, in many cases coals that did not burn completely can be used as fuel; and second, campfires often leave "scars" on the ground, such as the marks of the fire including the coals, the ash and also the low grasses next to the fire that the flames consume as it burns. It is unpleasant to sleep on this mess and unfortunately the overnight campsites are full of it, so it is better to use the remains of an existing campfire and not create additional "scars" in the area.
5. If there are no remains of existing campfires, dig a pit for the campfire. It is better to light the campfire in a pit, which will help contain it and later also cover it and remove the mess.
6. Make sure the campfire is not under a tree or next to bushes. To prevent sparks from reaching tree branches and low leaves, keep it away from them.

How do we light the fire? Matches or a lighter are the most convenient option. A fire can also be lit using a fire steel, but it is heavier and requires a high level of skill.
Gathering tinder: To light the campfire we will need flammable materials found around us. Dead, dry grasses, pine needles and even the toilet paper we used during the day. If nothing is available, you can use a good knife to cut thin wood shavings from the fuel we brought in advance, such as pieces of wood and pallets we planned to burn in the campfire.
Fuel: To protect the natural vegetation around the overnight campsite, we avoid at all costs breaking branches and damaging trees or bushes. Think for a moment what would happen if each and every one of us broke just one branch, and remember that even a rotting tree trunk decomposing on the ground has environmental meaning and importance – for example, it serves as a home and food for a variety of insects and fungi, which are part of the area's biodiversity.
The fuel needs to be dry, and it can be obtained by collecting leftovers from other campfires at the campsite and wooden pallets that jeep drivers sometimes leave behind, or through "caches". At the campsites in the south, in addition to water bottles, you can also buy sacks of firewood for campfires from the water-caching providers.
Lighting the campfire: Kneel next to the spot where we want to light the fire, and prepare piles of tinder and fuel to one side, in order. First, prepare a pile of the thinnest and most flammable tinder (such as wood shavings, pine needles or toilet paper). Then add small dry twigs we found on the ground, and finally the fuel that is meant to burn for a long time, such as planks.
There are various methods of fire engineering, and the simplest of all is probably the tepee or pyramid method. Pile up, from the inside out: easily ignited material at the bottom, and above it twigs from small to large. Make sure the whole time that the pyramid is ventilated enough for the oxygen essential for burning to get in.
Once the pyramid is ready, light the most flammable materials at the bottom. Usually, when done right, the fire catches and spreads from the most flammable materials to the twigs. In practice, sometimes you need to add more of the most flammable material until the fire catches on the twigs, or blow gently at the fire from below.
